utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could the case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is case number IT-04-82-T, The Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have had appearances, but I think as this is the commencement of the opening, we will take them again so that those watching are aware. Mr. Saxon, you appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues, Ms. Joanne Motoike; Mr. Matthias Neuner; Ms. Meritxell Regue; and our case manager to my left, Ms. Lakshima Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence, Edina Residovic, the defence counsel; Guenal Mettraux, co-counsel, Dragan Godzo, legal consultant; and Jesenka Residovic is legal assistant and case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence of Johan Tarculovski, appearing Antonio Apostolski, head counsel; Jasmina Zivkovic, co-counsel; and Jordan Apostolski, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will just confirm that firstly Mr. Boskoski is able to hear the proceedings in a language he understands? THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understand the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tarculovski? THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] I can understand it too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The purpose of this morning is to hear opening statements in this case, and I would therefore turn, first of all, to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Very briefly, before I begin my remarks today, I would just like to give you an outline of what the Prosecution intends to do. I will commence the Prosecution's opening remarks with a discussion regarding the existence of an armed conflict in the Republic of Macedonia during 2001. Then my colleague, Ms. Motoike, will describe the events that occurred in and around the village of Ljuboten between the 10th and 12th of August, 2001; as well as the criminal responsibility of the accused Tarculovski. I will then complete the remarks by a discussion of the evidence pertaining to the criminal responsibility of Mr. Boskoski. Before I begin, Your Honour, the Prosecution has prepared a number of copies of the court binder which we showed and discussed with the Trial Chamber at the pre-trial conference, and these binders have now been bound and copies have been made, and I'm wondering, with the assistance of the usher, whether copies could be distributed to the Judges and to co-counsel, because my colleague will be referring to one or more photographs in that binder during her remarks today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, there are several -- at least one or two, if not more, legal criteria which the Prosecution must establish in order to prove that an armed conflict, within the definition of international humanitarian law, existed in Macedonia at the relevant time period of the second amended indictment. First of all, the Prosecution must prove that there was sufficient organisation and structure of the belligerent Armed Forces so that each participating force had the ability to carry out military operations. Second, the Prosecution must demonstrate that the intensity of the armed violence or combat, if you will, rose to a certain level; that is, that the level of armed violence was something greater than mere banditry, common crime, or a disorganized or short-lived insurrection or terrorist activities, which are not subject to international humanitarian law. Thirdly, there is at least some authority that suggests that territorial control on the part of dissident armed groups, sufficient to enable them to carry out sustained and concerted military operations and to implement the additional protocol of the Geneva conventions might also be a legal requirement to establish the existence of an armed conflict. The Prosecution does not subscribe to this requirement, but, in any event, the Prosecution's evidence will establish that in this case the insurgent group that was fighting with the security forces of the Government of Macedonia, the National Liberation Army, took control of as much as 20 per cent of territory of Macedonia during 2001. The Prosecution's evidence will also establish the requisite nexus between the criminal conduct alleged in the second amended indictment and the armed conflict. Your Honours, the Republic of Macedonia, bordering Serbia and Albania, managed to avoid direct involvement in the armed conflicts which engulfed the Balkan region during the 1990s. It was only in 2001 that simmering inter-ethnic tensions between the Slavic-speaking ethnic Macedonian majority and the ethnic Albanian minority in Macedonia culminated in an internal armed conflict within the Macedonia borders. The parties to the conflict were the security forces of Macedonia the Government of Macedonia, comprising the Army of the Republic of Macedonia and the forces of the Ministry of Interior; and the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army, also known by its acronym, the NLA in English. Armed clashes between the parties commenced in January 2001 and rapidly developed into a protracted armed conflict, during which the NLA seized control of at least 20 per cent of the national territory. Following months of fierce fighting and unable to eliminate the NLA by force, the Macedonian government was forced to seek a negotiated political settlement. On the 13th of August, 2001, the Ohrid Framework Agreement was signed which precipitated the process of NLA disarmament and demobilization in exchange for constitutional and legislative amendments favourable to the ethnic Albanian minority. The NLA's Supreme Commander, Ali Achmete formally announced the NLA's dissolution on the 27th of September of 2001. Let me briefly describe to you some of the Prosecution's evidence pertaining to the first legal requirement, the level of organisation and structure of the participating Armed Forces. Your Honours, the Army of the Republic of Macedonia made up the bulk of the Macedonian government's forces and comprised more than 10.000 active-duty soldiers and a reserve contingent of up to 24.000 men. The army's weaponry included around 100 tanks, up to 100 armoured personnel carriers, several hundred cannons, Howitzers and mortars, as well as combat aircraft and antiaircraft weaponry. The army deployed all categories of conventional weapons during the armed conflict in 2001, including light weapons, artillery, armoured personnel carriers, tanks, combat helicopters, and fixed-wing aircraft. Of course, all of these army forces responded to a unified and functioning chain of command. I would like to show you two short video clips that demonstrate the use of some of the weaponry by the army of the Republic of Macedonia during the armed conflict in 2001. These clips are from Prosecution 65 ter number 985. They'll be shown without any sound. We see a tank firing at what are apparently NLA positions in that village. We see shells landing. And the next clip, which shows the use of mortars by the Army of the Republic of Macedonia, mortar shells striking what appear to be NLA positions on Mount Kala. Your Honours, the forces of the Ministry of Interior constituted the remainder of the forces under the command of the Macedonian government. Ministry of Interior forces, numbering approximately 9.700 police personnel, were active in the conflict areas and often engaged in joint operations with the army. Due to the rapidly deteriorating security situation in 2001, reserve personnel within the Ministry of Interior were mobilized, resulting in a total of 10.200, approximately, engaged reserve personnel at the height of the armed conflict. All of these forces were subordinate to and under the effective control of Ljube Boskoski after he became the Minister of Interior in May of 2001. The next video clip, which comes from Prosecution ter number 984, will also be shown without sound, was taken in the city of Tetovo in the spring of 2001, where there was fierce fighting between Macedonian government and -- the Macedonian government forces and the NLA. Can we see this clip, please? We see an armoured personnel carrier of the army going through the street. We see a -- either a soldier or a police officer firing a weapon at NLA positions above the city. And here we see a police officer firing his Kalashnikov at what are apparently NLA positions, and here a group of police officers firing, here an armoured personnel carrier moving through the city. Your Honours, opposing the Macedonian security forces was the National Liberation Army; in English known as the NLA, in Albanian with the acronym UCHEKA. The NLA was a political military organisation that traced its origins to various ethnic Albanian groups based in Kosovo and Macedonia since the 1980s, as well as in Europe. The NLA grew out of the Kosovo-Albanian militancy that followed the 1999 Kosovo war and NATO bombing campaign, as well as the grievances of the ethnic Albanian minority in Macedonia. Under the overall leadership of Ali Achmete, the NLA's numbers rapidly increased in 2001 to a force that peaked at about 6.000 men; mainly ethnic Albanian-Macedonia citizens, plus an unarmed reserve that provided support and logistics. The NLA was an organised armed force. The expert report of Viktor Bezruchenko, the Prosecution's military analyst, explains that it was comprised of four main components: The Supreme Command was the Supreme Commander and political representative, Mr. Achmete, plus support staff; the general staff; deployed fighting units; and an externally-associated organisation known as "Liria Kombetare," which is Albanian for the phrase "national freedom," which was responsible for the coordination of political and fundraising activities abroad. The most prominent individuals within the NLA leadership were Mr. Ali Achmete, also known as Abaz, the NLA Supreme Commander and political representative; Mr. Gzim Ostreni, also known as Plaku, who was the chief of NLA's General Staff; and Fazli Veliu, who was the NLA's coordinator of political activities for the Albanian Diaspora. If we can take a look now at a portion of 65 ter number 969. Your Honour, this sketch, which comes from a document from the military intelligence sector of the Macedonian Ministry of Defence describes how the military component of the NLA included the General Staff, with Gzim Ostreni at the top as its chief, as well as at least six combat brigades which vary in structure, strength and composition. You see from the left there was the 112th Brigade; the 116th Brigade; the 113th Brigade; the 114th Brigade, which operated in the area close to the village of Ljuboten; the 115th Brigade; and the 111th Brigade, all with commanders who reported up to the General Staff. The NLA had an identifiable hierarchy of command involving superior/subordinate relationships between the General Staff and Supreme Command and the brigades. All military activities were planned and coordinated by the General Staff, which exercised the NLA's command and control function. The Prosecution will adduce evidence to show the exercise of effective control over personnel and units and the use of headquarters and command posts, with the ability to plan and coordinate armed operations. Your Honours, command and control at the brigade level was facilitated by daily contacts between the brigade commanders and the NLA chief of General Staff, Gzim Ostreni. Lateral and vertical communications between brigades and the General Staff were maintained through satellite telephone communications. The NLA also had a crude logistic system and training areas. The NLA leaders made efforts to introduce common uniforms, insignia denoting rank and units, internal rules and regulations, and military police. NLA weaponry included mainly automatic and semi-automatic rifles, hand-held rocket-launchers, antiaircraft machine guns, portable surface-to-air missiles, antitank and antipersonnel mines and hand grenades. If we could turn to the Prosecution's 65 ter number 662, this is a page from a report from the Ministry of Interior's Security and? Counter-Intelligence Division, dated the 23rd of August, 2001, and if we can focus on the last -- the bottom half of that page, we see that the Ministry of the Interior noted that the NLA possessed over 100.000 pieces of weaponry, including 16.000 automatic rifles, 3.000 semi-automatic rifles, 2.000 sniper rifles, 3.000 light-machine guns, 20.000 hand grenades; hand-held rocket-launchers, et cetera, et cetera. Even Howitzers, 50 Howitzers at the bottom, and 100 antiaircraft cannons. Although the NLA's structure lacked the complex organisation of a modern conventional army, it nevertheless possessed all the basic elements of an organised armed force, a command element, combat units and logistical support elements. As a further indication of its strength and organisation, the NLA enjoyed external relations with the media and international organisations. The NLA issued communiques and political statements and met with representatives of the mediating parties preceding the conclusion of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. In summary, Your Honours, during all relevant times the NLA sufficiently possessed the characteristics of an organised, armed group capable of engaging in military operations. Let me turn now to the second legal requirement regarding the intensity of the armed conflict. As carefully detailed in Chapter 5 of the expert report of military analyst Viktor Bezruchenko, the armed violence in Macedonia during the period January to September 2001 reached the requisite threshold to prove the existence of an internal armed conflict. The intensity of the armed violence was characterised by the duration, frequency and the geographic scope of the violence; the territorial control of the warring parties; and the displacement of persons and the casualties that occurred. Furthermore, even early on the conflict was of such intensity that it attracted the attention of the United Nations Security Council and ultimately the intervention of NATO and the European union. I would like to show you a page or two from Prosecution 65 ter number 3, which is a publication by the Macedonian Ministry of Internal Affairs that is known as the white book, which contains a great deal of information about the conflict in 2001. But if we focus on the next page, please, and focus first on paragraph 1, we see that the Security Council, as early as March 2001, strongly condemns extremist violence, including terrorist activities in certain parts of the Republic of Macedonia and certain municipalities in Southern Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and notes that such violence has support from ethnic Albanian extremists outside these areas and constitutes a threat to the security and stability of the wider region. Can we go back to that page, please? And if we could now focus on paragraph 4, please. We see later on, in the same resolution, the Security Council demands that all those who are currently engaged in armed action against the authorities of those states immediately cease all such actions, lay down their weapons, and return to their homes. Your Honour -- Your Honours, a brief timeline of the armed conflict that again is summarised in detail in Chapter 5 to the Bezruchenko expert report provides an indication of the level of combat operations that took place between the NLA and Macedonian security forces from January through September 2001. For the convenience of everyone in the courtroom, the Prosecution has produced hard copies of two maps that also contained in Prosecution's 65 ter Exhibit number 3 the so-called white book, and I would like, if I could ask the assistance of the usher, perhaps to place one copy on the ELMO so that my colleagues can follow along as well as the Judges. The reason we are working with hard copies on the ELMO, Your Honours, is because on the computer screen simply the quality of the map appears of a low quality. Your Honours, beginning in January of 2001, the NLA launched an attack against government forces in a village called Tearce, which is to the north of the city of Tetovo, close to the border between Kosovo and Macedonia. Clashes in the area of Tanusevci, a village to the north of the city of Skopje along the border with Kosovo and Macedonia took place in February 2001. During March of 2001, NLA attacks on Macedonian security forces occurred in the area of Kudra Fura, Caska, Malino and Brest on the borders with Serbia. Further clashes continued in the area of Tanusevci, but the most intensive fighting took place in the area of Tetovo and surrounding villages. And if you look at the map, on the bottom half of the page that I've given to you, you'll see a number of red stars indicating villages in and around the city of Tetovo that were the scene of fighting beginning in March 2001. The situation prompted government forces to launch an offensive operation in the area of Tetovo in the second half of March, with heavy fighting in the area of Kale, Lavce, Selce, Gajre, Germo, Sipkovica, Vejce and Brodec to the west of Tetovo. In May 2001, Your Honours, if you take a look at the map on the upper part of the page, you see the city of Kumanovo to the northeast of Skopje, and in the May of that year the NLA opened up another front in the area of Kumanovo by taking control of the village of Vaksince, which is to the northeast of the city of Kumanovo. The NLA took control of one village after another, including Slupcane, Lojane and Matejce, gradually pushing to the west towards Skopje. For those reasons, the Macedonian security forces launched an offensive operation against the NLA in the area of Vaksince and Slupcane. Your Honours, between February and June 2001, the NLA established control over considerable territory in the areas adjacent to the borders with Serbia, starting from the villages of Brest and Malino and in the mountains around Tetovo. In June of 2001, the NLA extended its northern front to just 10 kilometres from the city of Skopje, which you see here in the middle of the map. The NLA took control of the Skopje suburb of Aricinovo, which is located to the east of Skopje, and also expanded the area -- its area of control around the border town of Radusha. In July, 2001, the fighting continued on all fronts. The NLA took control of additional villages around Tetovo. In August of 2001, the NLA took control or, shall I say perhaps cut the strategic Skopje-Tetovo highway running from east to west between those two cities. NLA soldiers moved freely along the highway and established check-points in the area. The city of Tetovo was on the verge of falling to the NLA forces, and there was street fighting in parts of the city and NLA check-points established within the urban area. The urgency and the seriousness of that situation prompted then President Trajkovski to order a military operation to regain control of the highway and to prevent the seizure of Tetovo itself. On the 10th of August, 2001, eight Macedonian soldiers died in a mine explosion to the north of the village of Ljuboten. All of these details are described in Chapter 5 of the expert report of Viktor Bezruchenko, as well in other exhibits that the Prosecution will provide to you during the course of the trial. In the course of the conflict, Your Honours, the NLA succeeded in establishing control, as I've said before, of up to 20 per cent of the territory of Macedonia, mainly in the northern and northwestern regions. If we can see a page from what would be Prosecution's 65 ter number 410 - I'm grateful to Ms. Walpita for her efficiency - this page comes from the annual report of the Ministry of the Interior for 2001. And if we can focus, please, on the first paragraph. In other words, this report was published in the beginning of 2002, looking back to the events of 2001, by the Ministry of The Interior. By that time, the Minister was still the accused in this case, Mr. Boskoski. And you see at the top of the paragraph: "As a consequence of the armed activities of the Albanian terrorist organisation, the so-called NLA, in the course of 2001 in the northwest part of the Republic of Macedonia, 20 per cent of her territory was temporarily occupied." Your Honours, the territorial control achieved by the NLA was sufficient to allow and support sustained and concerted military operations and was characterised by a degree of stability in the areas controlled, to the exclusion of government forces. Territorial control of the NLA was evident in the establishment of check-points and road barricades; the free deployment of NLA units from one location to another; the reinforcement of NLA defence positions and the strengthening of their fortifications; the establishment of so-called authority bodies in so-called liberated areas. And if we look again at the first paragraph on this page from Exhibit 410, the report of the Ministry of the Interior, we see 69 members of the security forces were murdered, as well as 16 civilians; 174 members of the Minister of Internal affairs and 211 members of the Army of the Republic of Macedonia were wounded. Property damage of a large scale was over half a billion -- was -- excuse me, was 150 million Euros by arson, destruction and damage, but damage to the economy was estimated at over half a billion Euros. Lower down, we see that over 86.000 citizens on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia were displaced from their homes and settlements, and 80.000 citizens left the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and temporarily stayed abroad. Over 40 religious facilities were damaged. Your Honours, this conflict involved frequent and intensive armed clashes which occurred virtually continuously between January and September 2001 over a widespread and expanding geographic area. Although the NLA forces were less numerous than the government forces, the evidence will show that the conflict was not one-sided. NLA attacks were carried out against a variety of Macedonian military targets over a wide and expanding area of Macedonia. Furthermore, NLA forces were able to offer strong and often effective resistance to Macedonian forces undertaking military and police operations. While large numbers of well-equipped Macedonian forces were deployed in the relevant areas of Macedonia during the period relevant to the second amended indictment, the NLA enjoyed a significant level of overall military success, tying up the Macedonian security forces with effective guerrilla-style tactics. In conclusion, Your Honours, the Prosecution will adduce sufficient evidence to prove that at all relevant times an armed conflict existed in Macedonia for the purposes of the application of international humanitarian law, and that a nexus existed between that armed conflict and the crimes that occurred in and around the village of Ljuboten in August of 2001. With your leave, Your Honours, I will now turn the podium over to my colleague, Ms. Motoike, for another section of the Prosecution's opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As Mr. Saxon indicated, I'm going to speak about the events in Ljuboten with respect to the second amended indictment, and then I'll turn to the criminal responsibility of Johan Tarculovski. With respect to the events in Ljuboten, could we see a picture, please, of Ljuboten village, which is on the fifth page of the court binder? It's identified by ERNNOO57603. This is a panoramic photo from the southeastern viewpoint of Ljuboten village. Ljuboten is a small village which sits at the southwestern foot of the Skopska Crna Gora mountain ridge in the northern part of Macedonia. It is about 10 kilometres by air from the centre of Skopje, which is the capital of Macedonia. Most of the residents in Ljuboten are ethnic Albanians who are mainly farmers by profession. The village is surrounded by three predominantly ethnic Macedonian villages: Ljubanci to the northwest; Rastak to the southeast; and Radushane, which is to the southwest. The Prosecution will present evidence that in the early morning hours on Sunday, 12th August 2001, this picturesque village and its residents were subjected to an intense, brutal and unlawful attack for which the accused are criminally responsible. Before speaking of this attack, however, a brief summary of the events that occurred just prior to the 12th of August is necessary. On 10 August 2001, two days before this unlawful attack, a Macedonian military vehicle belonging to the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Guardist Brigade was destroyed by a remote-controlled explosive device in an ambush. This occurred in a place called Ljubotenski Bacila, which is in the Skopska Crna Gora mountain ridge area about 5 kilometres north of Ljuboten. This vehicle was carrying an outgoing shift of soldiers of the second company to Ljubanci. Unfortunately, eight soldiers were killed in the incident; two of whom were residents of Ljubanci. The Prosecution will present evidence that immediately following the explosion, members of the National Liberation Army or NLA opened fire on the Macedonian military vehicle, causing the Macedonian Army's 2nd Company to respond. These two groups exchanged fire for several hours that day. Afterwards, the 3rd Battalion of the Macedonian Army opened small-arms fire on the village of Ljuboten. Two mortar and/or cannon rounds were also launched into Ljuboten presumably in retaliation for the death of the eight soldiers. The rounds killed two Ljuboten civilians; one of them a five-year-old child. The evidence will show that at the time the army opened fire that Friday, there were no legitimate military targets in the village, other than possibly a group of three armed persons, yet no hostile or defensive acts were committed by these persons or any residents of Ljuboten. The Prosecution will show that later on the same day, a police unit, commanded by the accused Johan Tarculovski, arrived in the neighbouring village of Ljubanci and during the night hours on Friday this unit conducted a reconnaissance of Ljuboten. Evidence will show that on Saturday morning, the 11th of August, the Macedonian army again opened small-arms fire on Ljuboten, and later that evening members of Johan Tarculovski's police unit fired several rockets into the village. At the time of these actions, there were no legitimate military targets in the village. Additionally, no hostile or defensive acts had been committed towards the army or this police unit by the residents of Ljuboten. In the early morning hours of the next day, which was Sunday, 12 August 2001, the intense, unlawful ground attack on Ljuboten commenced. The evidence will show that at approximately 8.00 that morning, Johan Tarculovski's police unit, comprised of about 100 men, entered the northwestern end of Ljubanci -- of Ljuboten from Ljubanci. If we could see a photo from Prosecution's 65 ter 199, this photograph, Your Honours, is also photo A on page 8 of the court binder. This is an aerial photograph of the northwestern and northeastern parts of Ljuboten village. Your Honours, with the leave of the Court, I have pre-marked the photographs I will be utilising and displaying in my statement in an effort to save time. The red line in this photograph, if followed from the right of the photograph to the left, indicates the path of this unit. Their point of entry into Ljuboten is marked with a "1" and a red circle. The evidence will show that this assault focused mainly on the northern and eastern parts of the village, which in relation to this photograph that's being displayed is the bottom half. As the unit advanced into the village, witnesses will testify that this -- that the Macedonian army, excuse me, provided fire support for this police ground assault by firing mortar and cannon rounds into and around the village between approximately 6.00 and 10.00 in the morning. Evidence will further show that this shelling was calculated to dissolve any possible resistance to the advancing police unit led by the accused Tarculovski. The Prosecution will present witness testimony that at approximately 8.20 that morning, members of this police unit forcibly entered the yard of Jusufi household. This household is in the northwestern part of Ljuboten. If we could see another photo, which is actually a closer shot of the northwestern part of Ljuboten, from 65 ter 199. This is also photo A on page 9 of the court binder. In this photograph, the red line again traces the point of entry from the right of the photograph to the left. The red circle labelled "1" indicates the point of entry of the unit, and the red circle labelled "2" marks the location of the Jusufi household. Rami Jusufi, a 33-year-old ethnic Albanian, was asleep in his bed when his mother called him to the front door of their house. When he got up and went to the door, he was shot by at least one of the police officers in the yard. Rami Jusufi was unarmed. He fell from his wounds and was dragged by his 57-year-old mother from the doorway. Two hours later, in the presence of his family, Rami Jusufi died. After the killing of Rami Jusufi, the evidence will show that this police unit then moved to the upper eastern part of Ljuboten where they arrived at the houses of Adem Ametovski and Zija Ademi at about 11:00 o'clock in the morning. Can we see the previous photo of the northeastern and northwestern portion of Ljuboten from 65 ter 199? Again, Your Honours, this is photo A on page 8 of the court binder. The eastern portion of the village is in the lower half of this photo, while the western portion is depicted in the upper half. If one follows the red line in this photograph from the left to the right, the line indicates the path this unit took. Again, the red circle marked with a "1" indicates the point of entry for the unit, while the red circle marked with a "3" in the photograph indicates the location of the Ametovski and Ademi homes. At these two homes, men, women and children, all unarmed and all ethnic Albanian, were seeking cover in the basements from the police ground attack and the shelling by the army. Most of the men were in the basement of the Ametovski house, while the women and children were sheltering in the basement of the Ademi house. The police ordered the men out from these basements and detained 13 of them near the main gate of the Ametovski house. The detained men, including one juvenile male, were forced to lie on the ground, where they were punched, kicked, jumped on and hit by the police with rifle butts and wooden sticks. One police officer even carved a large cross into the back of another detainee. The beatings left these men with multiple injuries to their heads and bodies. Witnesses will testify that at some point during these beatings, one of the detainees, Sulejman Bajrami, a 23-year-old ethnic Albanian, stood up and began to either run or walk away. As he did so, he was shot and killed by at least one police officer while his younger brother and father watched. Witnesses will also testify that at some point, Sulejman's father, Aziz Bajrami, was shot in the hand. After the killing of Sulejman Bajrami, two of the men, including a juvenile, were then forced to walk under armed escort and continued beatings to the adjoining village of Ljubanci. Two men from the group, apparently due to their elderly age, were ordered to leave. But as they walked away, members of the police unit fired at them, killing one, Muharem Ramadani, a 65-year-old ethnic Albanian resident. I apologise, Your Honours, if I misspoke. I didn't mean to say "two men" if that's what I did say, I meant to say ten of the men, including the juvenile, were then forced to walk under armed escort. The evidence will show that these ten males were escorted along the west-east road in Ljuboten. If we could see the same aerial photo of the northeast and northwest parts of Ljuboten from 65 ter 199. Again, it's photo A of page 8 on the court binder. As indicated previously, the red circle marked with a "3" in this photograph shows the location where these males were detained. As one follows the red line from this circle, from the left of the photograph to the right, the line marks the route these males were forced to take out of the village to Ljubanci. It is essentially the same route this police unit took into the village. Ljubanci is situated just to the right of the location marked with a red circle and the number "1" on the photograph. The males were escorted to the police check-point at a residence known as Braca's house, which is situated at the edge of the Ljuboten and the adjacent village of Ljubanci. Braca's house is surrounded by a concrete fence which witnesses will refer to as the Chinese wall. Witnesses will testify that at Braca's house, the beatings by members of this police unit continued for about half an hour. The males continued to be kicked on, jumped on, and some were even hit with pieces of burning wood. Again, many suffered multiple injuries to their bodies as a result. Afterwards, the males were forcibly thrown onto a police truck and taken to Mirkovci police station. A witness will testify that upon arrival at the station, some of the males were simply tossed off the truck onto the concrete driveway. From that point, which was the 12th of August, until the 14th of August, the males were subjected to even more physical abuse by regular and reserve police officers in and outside of this police station. This abuse resulted in even more injuries to those already suffering. The Prosecution will present evidence that one of these males eventually died as a result of these beatings. Witnesses will testify that Atula Qaili, a 35-year-old ethnic Albanian, was one of the remaining ten males who were forced to walk from the Ametovski house to Braca's house on 12th August. En route, he was continually beaten. Consequently, when he arrived at Braca's house, Mr. Qaili was in a seriously injured state. Nonetheless, the evidence will show that members of this police unit kicked him repeatedly at the check-point and threw him into the back of an open police truck with the other males. Like the others, he was taken to the Mirkovci police station where the beatings continued. These repeated beatings left Mr. Qaili battered and unable to speak. He was then transported to Skopje City Hospital where he died on 13 August 2001 as a result of his injuries. The Prosecution will present expert evidence that Mr. Qaili's injuries were consistent with the use of objects and/or mechanical tools on the body of Mr. Qaili, and that these injuries were the result of his death. Following the murders of Rami Jusufi, Sulejman Bajrami and Muharem Ramadani, and while the ten males were being marched off, beaten and detained at Braca's house, the police unit continued to move further east through the village to the house of Qani Jushari. Could we see another photo of Ljuboten village, which is 65 ter 199. This is also photo D, Your Honours, on page 8 of the court binder. The bottom half of this photo illustrates the southeastern part of Ljuboten village. The red circle marked with a "3" indicates the location of the Ametovski and Ademi homes. If one follows the red line from the circle marked with a "3" to the red circle marked with a "4," this indicates the path the unit took to the Jashari house that day. Witnesses will testify that at the Jashari house, five unarmed men had sought refuge from the advancing police unit. When the police arrived at the Jashari house, witnesses will testify that the police opened fire on the home and then used petrol to set both the house and the barn on fire. The five unarmed men, who were seeking refuge at this house, then jumped out of the home's side window and hid a short distance away in the adjacent field. But when these men were spotted, the police opened fire. The men continued to flee through the open field towards the mountains. The evidence will show that as these men ran up into the field, the police shot and killed three of them: Xhelal Bajrami, Bajram Jashari and Kadri Jashari, all ethnic Albanians. The other two men, (redacted) escaped; one injured by a bullet and the other unharmed. The Prosecution will also present evidence that the police unit, led by the accused Tarculovski, burned houses and left a trail of physical destruction as they progressed in Ljuboten that fateful Sunday. The unit set fire to and damaged at least 14 houses by using hand grenades and small-arms. In the northern, upper eastern and eastern parts of the village, police set fire to a number of homes with petrol, while they opened fire at others with small-arms. Video taken on that day illustrates this path of destruction. Could we see a clip, please, from 65 ter 309? This is video coverage of Ljuboten from that day, where Your Honours could see homes burning, obviously smoke arising from the village from a distance away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution will present evidence of an independent assessment conducted by an international housing reconstruction group in September of 2001. This assessment will describe the type and extent of the damage to these homes. The evidence will further indicate that none of these houses were occupied by combatants and none were used as a point of resistance in the village by its residents. Indeed, the evidence will show that this destruction was completely wanton, intentional, and committed without any military justification. In addition to the beatings and visible destruction in the village of Ljuboten, witnesses will also testify as to the cruel treatment of many other Albanian men, including at least one juvenile male from Ljuboten at the Buzalak check-point on 12 August 2001. On the 12th, villagers fled Ljuboten with their families by heading towards the city of Skopje. Video from that day illustrates this. Could we see a clip, please, from 65 ter 309? Your Honours, this is video footage shot near Buzalak check-point on 12 August 2001, which shows the line of villagers from Ljuboten heading towards Skopje. Thank you. Evidence will show that between the early afternoon and 6:00 o'clock in the evening on 12 August 2001, ethnic Albanian men who arrived at Buzalak check-point were arrested at gunpoint as they fled the village with their families. Witnesses will testify that these men were beaten by regular and reserve police, as well as some civilians who acted at the encouragement of the police. They were beaten repeatedly, sometimes with objects such as rifle butts and wooden sticks. Evidence will also show that one ethnic Albanian man was shot in the head as he and another male ran away from the check-point in fear. Video shot on that day will confirm this account. Can we see the clip from 65 ter 309, please? This is more footage from the area near Buzalak check-point, showing the man had actually already fallen from being shot in the head, while the other man ran. Thank you. The Prosecution will present evidence that the men detained at Buzalak check-point suffered multiple injuries as a result of such beatings. Permanent disabilities resulted from some of the injuries received by the detainees. Due to the nature of some of their injuries, a number of these detainees have also lost their ability to work and support their families. Witnesses will also testify to the cruel treatment of ethnic Albanian men from Ljuboten at other locations in and outside the city of Skopje on the 12th of August. That afternoon detainees from Buzalak check-point were taken in separate groups to Cair, Kisela Voda and Bit Pazar and Karpos police stations. Witnesses will further testify that at these locations, these detainees were beaten by regular and reserve police officers in and outside of these various police stations during their detention and upon their arrival and departure. As with the other beatings, these were often committed with instruments. The Prosecution will also present evidence that the beatings for some detainees continued even after being transported to Skopje Court 2 for initial court appearances. On 14 August 2001, several detainees were brought for the initial court appearance at Skopje Court 2. While there, some of them were beaten in the hallways and corridors of the court. They were beaten by regular reserve police, prison guards, and some civilians with the permission and encouragement of the police and guards. Evidence will also be presented that these beatings continued even after some detainees were transported for treatment to Skopje City Hospital. Between 12 and 21 August 2001, badly injured ethnic Albanian detainees were brought from various locations to Skopje City Hospital. Some of these detainees will testify that they were beaten in front of the hospital or in their rooms by regular and reserve police, and by hospital personnel who mistreated the detainees while the police officers stood by. This evidence will show that the detention and beatings of these men were organised, systematic and pervasive. Indeed, most of the detainees were beaten repetitively at successive locations as some were transported from one station to another, and physically abused at each station. Through the presentation of this evidence, the Prosecution will prove beyond a reasonable doubt the crimes of murder, wanton destruction, and cruel treatment as alleged in the second amended indictment. Next, I'd like to speak about the criminal liability of the accused Johan Tarculovski. The evidence presented by the Prosecution will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Tarculovski is responsible under Article 7(1) of the statue for the crimes described in the second amended indictment. At the time of the attack on Ljuboten, the accused Tarculovski was a 26-year-old police officer employed by the Ministry of Interior as a bodyguard to the president's security unit. At the time, he was a member of the same political party to which the accused Ljube Boskoski belonged. The Prosecution will present evidence in the form of documents and witness testimony that about two weeks before the attack on Ljuboten in July 2001, Ljube Boskoski ordered Johan Tarculovski to select a group of individuals who would be under Johan Tarculovski's leadership to participate in a police security operation. Johan Tarculovski personally selected individuals from the regular and reservist police force to participate in this operation. Some of the individuals selected by Johan Tarculovski were also members of Kometa, a private security agency with which Johan Tarculovski had close ties. The evidence will show that these members of Kometa were hired and activated as reservists after being selected by Johan Tarculovski. The Prosecution will also present evidence that the accused Tarculovski organised the arming and outfitting of these selected individuals with semi-automatic weapons and pistols, which was approved by the accused Boskoski. Evidence will be further presented that on 10 August 2001, with tensions extremely high following the killing of the eight Macedonian soldiers at Ljubotenski Bacila, the accused Boskoski ordered Johan Tarculovski to conduct a search of Ljuboten village for Xhavid Asani. The evidence will show that Ljube Boskoski believed Mr. Asani to have been responsible for the killing of the eight soldiers, and Ljube Boskoski believed Mr. Asani was hiding in Ljuboten. Johan Tarvulovski was selected because he knew the area of Ljuboten well, as he had a family home in the adjoining village of Ljubanci. The Prosecution will present documentation and witness testimony to show that the accused Tarculovski, acting on this order, then selected around 100 men from the active and reserve police, as well as employees from the security company, Kometa. During the afternoon of 10 August 2001, the evidence will show that Johan Tarculovski then commenced the planning and preparation for the unlawful attack on the village of Ljuboten. Witnesses will testify that Johan Tarculovski arrived at Cair police station with about 50 men dressed in camouflage police uniforms and armed with weapons. Upon arrival, Johan Tarculovski requested that officers stationed at Cair transport these 50 men to the school building in Ljubanci, home to two of the soldiers killed by the explosive device the same day. Witnesses will also testify on this same date that a Ministry of Interior truck driven by police arrived at the Ljubanci school to deliver ammunition, bombs and grenade launchers, which were then distributed to between 60 and 70 persons who had come to this location. Over the course of these two days, which were the 10th and 11th of August, 2001, evidence will show that Johan Tarculovski attended at least two meetings and had several communications with the military and police officials responsible for the police and army security for the area. Documentary evidence and witness testimony will show that at these meetings and through these communications, Johan Tarculovski demanded more weapons and logistical support from the army and the police. During the later meeting on the 11th of August, Johan Tarculovski advised these officials that he would be leading the attack against Ljuboten, which would commence on 12 August 2001 at 4.30 in the morning, regardless of the support from the Macedonian army. In the early evening hours of that Saturday, which was the 11th of August, evidence will show that the police unit commanded by the accused Tarculovski used grenade launchers to set the houses in Ljuboten on fire. Witnesses will testify that on the following Sunday morning, 12 August 2001, the accused Tarculovski did indeed lead this unlawful ground attack on Ljuboten. The attack began with mortar fire into Ljuboten at the request of the accused, Tarculovski. The Prosecution will present witness testimony that following the mortar attack, the accused Tarculovski also contacted Mr. Boskoski to request the use of a armoured vehicle from the Ministry of Interior. This vehicle was to provide cover to Johan Tarculovski's police unit. Evidence will show that the accused Boskoski, then ordered the implementation of this request. As described previously, the evidence will show that the police unit, led by the accused Tarculovski, deliberately killed unarmed civilians, wantonly burned and destroyed many homes without justification, and cruelly treated a group of residents, seven of whom were killed. During the unlawful ground attack, evidence will be presented that Johan Tarculovski was the leader of the unit into the village and was present during the unlawful attack. Consequently, the evidence will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the actions of the accused, Tarculovski, and the police unit he led in the village clearly had a criminal design, as demonstrated by the manner, method and results of their attack. The illegal objective of this joint criminal enterprise or JCE, was to direct an unlawful attack on civilians and on civilian objects in the village of Ljuboten, an attack that was not justified by military necessity. From the first moment when this police unit entered the village on Sunday, 12th August 2001, and Rami Jusufi was murdered, the evidence will show that the illegal nature of the attack was obvious. The criminal nature -- the criminal attack, excuse me, continued with the further murders of two unarmed civilian residents, Sulejman Bajrami and Muharem Ramadani. The final gunning down and killing on the same date of three additional unarmed Ljuboten residents, Xhelal Bajrami, Kadri Jashari and Bajram Jashari, will be further evidence of the criminal nature of this attack. Other documentary and witness evidence will be presented by the Prosecution indicating the existence of this JCE and its unlawful purpose. The Prosecution will show, through documentary evidence, that the police within the Ministry of Interior, had a systematic and comprehensive reporting system within the Ministry up to and after this unlawful attack. However, the evidence will show that despite this system, there was a lack of detailed reporting about the plans and activities eventually undertaken in Ljuboten that fateful weekend. Additionally, the Prosecution will present evidence that the three weapons, supposedly seized by the police at the Jashari house during this unlawful attack, were subsequently used to substantiate criminal charges against the persons detained at the Ametovski house, which was in another part of Ljuboten. The existence and unlawful purpose of the JCE will also be demonstrated through witness testimony and documentary evidence relating to the medical records for certain ethnic Albanian detainees from Ljuboten. The evidence the Prosecution will present, regarding the destruction of houses along the path followed by the police, also substantiates the criminal intent that members of the unit possessed as they moved through the village. Indicative of the criminal nature of the JCE was the police unit's killing of the unarmed civilians in Ljuboten and the cruel treatment of the males who were detained from the Ametovski house, which ultimately led to the death of one of the detainees, Atula Qaili. The Prosecution will also present evidence that this unlawful ground attack on civilians by the police was planned at or after the time that Ljube Boskoski ordered Johan Tarculovski and the police unit to go to the Ljuboten to search for Xhavid Asani. From the distinctly criminal nature of the entire operation, the plan would have had to have been in place before the police entered the village or, at the very least, developed extremely rapidly after the first crimes were committed. The witness and documentary evidence will prove that the accused Tarculovski participated in this JCE as a co-perpetrator. As discussed previously, the evidence will show that he was the central figure responsible for the attack, as his acts determined when and how the village would be attacked. He drew on resources, personnel and logistics, as required them, and he was the leader of and present with the police unit as it moved and committed crimes throughout the village. Alternatively, the same evidence will show that the crimes enumerated in Counts 1, 2 and 3 of the second amended indictment were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the objective of the JCE and that the accused Tarculovski was aware that such crimes were the possible consequences of the execution of the JCE. With that awareness, he nonetheless decided to participate in the enterprise. In addition to his participation in the JCE as described previously, the evidence will also show that the accused Tarculovski is individually criminally responsible for ordering, planning, instigating and aiding and abetting the crimes in the second amended indictment. Indeed, by virtue of the authority vested in him by the accused Boskoski, and by virtue of the central role that the accused Tarculovski played in the planning, preparation and execution of the attack on the village, Johan Tarculovski had the authority to issue orders to carry out the attack. The evidence will show that the accused Tarculovski ordered the crimes and the attack, or at least he acted with the awareness of the substantial likelihood that the crimes would be committed in the execution of his orders. On the basis of this evidence, the Prosecution will show beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Tarculovski is responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute for having committed, ordered, planned, instigated or otherwise aided and abetted the crimes in the second amended indictment. I would now like to turn the floor back over to my colleague, Mr. Saxon, who will speak about Ljube Boskoski's criminal responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the hour, and I wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would like an early break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, my comments, Your Honour, will take, I believe, approximately an hour, so this might be a good time to take the break, and then I should finish before noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will take the first break now, which will take half an hour, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I will now speak about the criminal responsibility of the accused Ljube Boskoski pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. During the afternoon of 12 August 2001, while the ethnic Albanian residents of Ljuboten were being beaten, abused and detained, Ljube Boskoski, then the Minister of the Interior for Macedonia and the superior of all police forces operating within that Ministry, arrived at the place referred to as Braca's house in the second amended indictment. This home and enclosed garden is on the outskirts of the village of Ljuboten. From behind a wall known as the Chinese wall, Mr. Boskoski was able to view the ongoing attack by his police forces in Ljuboten. I'd like to show a clip from Prosecution 65 ter 309 which shows Mr. Boskoski at that spot on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see smoke coming from the village of Ljuboten. You see the view from that Chinese wall; the police officer behind the wall; the inside of the garden; the arrival; you see fire-arms that were allegedly seized at Ljuboten that day, and you'll hear more about these fire-arms. There we see Mr. Boskoski at that so-called Chinese wall in Braca's house, and he's pointing to the direction of the ongoing activities in Ljuboten. If we can continue, please. There we see again the view that Mr. Boskoski would have had from that spot. Again we see smoke rising from the village of Ljuboten. Several witnesses will also describe seeing Mr. Boskoski at this spot on the 12th of August after they were detained by police officers, beaten, and forced to walk to Braca's house. In addition to Mr. Boskoski's personal presence at Ljuboten during the attack, additional Prosecution evidence will demonstrate his knowledge of the events that occurred at that village on the 12th of August, 2001. Witnesses will testify that on the 12th of August, Mr. Boskoski met with participants in the attack, such as the accused Johan Tarculovski, and in the evening he met with other participants of the joint criminal enterprise, such as Zoran Juvanovski, also known as Bucik, the owner of the security agency called Kometa. A limited number of police and Ministry of Interior reports about the events in Ljuboten were sent up the chain of command. If we can look briefly at 65 ter 224, Your Honours, this is a report sent to the Ministry of Interior, Internal Affairs Sector in Skopje on the 11th of August, 2001, regarding the security situation in the city for the period of 0800 to 2000 hours on the 11th of August. And if we go to the next page, we see at the top, from OVR-Cair, which at that time was the police department that for the municipality of Cair which had within its jurisdiction, Ljuboten, and you see a note that between 0800 and 10:00 o'clock in the morning, from above the ridge in the recreation ground in the village of Ljubanci, the Army of the Republic of Macedonia used infantry weapons to fire single shots and bursts of fire in the direction of the village of Ljuboten. If we can look at 65 ter number 217, please. This is a note signed by the supervisor of the OVR-Cair police station. It's dated the 12th of August 2001, and if we can highlight that paragraph, please. And it's a report -- if we can actually get the title as well. Thank you. A report on recorded events and measures undertaken regarding the Operation Ramno. This is a code word, Your Honours, that you will see in a number of documents that will be presented during the trial by the Prosecution, and the word Ramno simply referred to operations taken by the police that were related to the armed conflict then ongoing in 2001. And we see that in this note, in a conversation with the commander of the police station at Mirkovci, which fell within the jurisdiction of Cair, Slavko Ivanovski had asked to undertaken security measures regarding the safe return of inhabitants of the village of Ljuboten. If we can leave that exhibit now and move to Exhibit 232, please. Again, this is a document, it's dated the 12th of August, 2001, it's directed to the Internal Affairs Sector of the Minister of the Interior in Skopje. It's another report on events and measures taken with respect to Ramno. And if we can focus in on the text of the report, please. It's from the head of the OVR-Cair. And we see, for example, that at 10:00 o'clock in the morning a group of individuals was seen leaving the village of Ljuboten. In the next paragraph, shots were fired and bursts of fire from infantry weapons in the direction of the village of Ljuboten, et cetera. And if we can look at one more document, which would be Exhibit 232 -- oh, that perhaps would be 243. Go back, please. This should be 243, yes, 65 ter number 243. Your Honour, the date says "1 August 2001" at the top, but that must be a typographical error, because this is another report related to Operation Ramno from the supervisor of the OVR-Cair police station, and if we focus on the middle paragraph, you see a list of names, and these are -- this list of persons is a group of persons who were detained at Ljuboten on the 12th of August, and this is what the supervisor is reporting about it. Moreover, the events in Ljuboten received a great deal of media attention after the 12th of August, and the Prosecution during the trial will show you a number of media reports that include comments by Mr. Boskoski himself as they were reported in the Macedonian media, and furthermore international organisations, such as Human Rights Watch and the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhumane Treatment, published reports about the events in Ljuboten. Human Rights Watch published its formal report on the 6th of September 2001. If we can go to 65 ter number 355, please, the next exhibit. Next page, next page. This is the page of the -- first page of the report that was published by Human Rights Watch called "Crimes Against Civilians: Abuses by Macedonian Forces in Ljuboten, August 10 to 12, 2001." If we can go to page 2 of this report, please, the next page. And if we focus, first of all, on the third paragraph in the summary, we see that Human Rights Watch recorded, among other things, that Macedonian police forces committed serious abuses during their three-day operation in Ljuboten. Lower down, they say: "During their Sunday house-to-house attack, police forces shot dead six civilians. One man was killed by police as he tried to close the door to his home when the police entered the yard," et cetera. If we can go back to page 2, please, and focus on the fifth paragraph. We see Human Rights Watch also reported about the cruel treatment that occurred that day. You see they wrote: "The abuse continued for the hundreds of ethnic Albanian civilians who tried to flee Ljuboten." Lower down: "Over 100 men were arrested and taken to police stations in Skopje where they were subjected to severe beatings." It says to "Atula Qaili" -- it should say: "Atula Qaili, age 35, was taken away alive from the village by police officers, and his badly beaten and mutilated corpse was later recovered by family members from the city morgue." If we can go to the next page of the report, please. In the fourth paragraph here, if we can -- no, just the fourth paragraph there. In the first recommendation of the report, Human Rights Watch asks the Macedonian government to investigate and prosecute the persons responsible for the abuses in Ljuboten and to conduct credible, impartial and transparent investigation into the allegations of government abuses in Ljuboten, including the role of Minister of the Interior Ljube Boskoski and the forces under his command. Your Honours, prior to the publication of that report, however, in late August 2001, reports circulated in the "Sunday Telegraph" newspaper in London about the expected conclusions of the Human Rights Watch report which was then imminent, including concerns about the role and responsibility of the Ljube Boskoski for the crimes that occurred in the village of Ljuboten. If we can see 65 ter number 120, please. This is the text of a radio broadcast from Skopje radio Macedonia on the 27th of August, 2001, and if we can highlight this paragraph in the middle, please, starting with the word "Boskoski," it contains a response by the accused to the expected findings of Human Rights Watch. According to this report, Mr. Boskoski said: "I vigorously refute the accusations against the Interior Ministry, against the regular and the reserve police forces, which have demonstrated unprecedented courage in defending Macedonia's sovereignty and territorial integrity in the past six months. I view the accusations issued by the Human Rights Watch as a classic act of framing the Interior Minister, because their information is based on certain witnesses' claims, according to which I sat on a balcony observing a massacre of the civilian population. I fiercely refute these allegations. I am prepared to account for Macedonia at all times. My purpose here is to defend the Macedonian people's national interests, and I have no intention to justify my concrete actions. If there exists any evidence, I am prepared to account for it, although all this is out of the question." Therefore, the Prosecution will present overwhelming evidence, Your Honour, that Ljube Boskoski knew or had reason to know that his subordinates had committed the crimes alleged in the second amended indictment. Of course, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute, the Prosecution must prove that Mr. Boskoski exercised effective control over these subordinates. The defence do not dispute that at the time of the unlawful attack on Ljuboten, Ljube Boskoski was the Minister of the Interior of Macedonia and a member of one of the governing political parties. Mr. Boskoski held this position, the highest position of authority in the Ministry of Interior, from May of 2001 until November of 2002. In his capacity as the Minister of the Interior, Ljube Boskoski had the overall authority and responsibility for the functioning of the regular, reserve, and special police forces within the Ministry of the Interior. He exercised de jure and de facto effective control over these police forces, which included Johan Tarculovski and the police unit that directly participated in the crimes charged in the indictment. Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski's de jure authority over police forces came from several sources. First of all, I'd like to draw your attention to Prosecution 65 ter number 93, which was the Macedonian constitution that was enforced in 2001. And if we focus on Article 95 for a moment, we see in Article 95, paragraph 1, that the state administration consists of ministers and other administrative bodies and organisations determined by law. If we turn now to 65 ter number 95, which is the law on the organisation and work of government bodies, and we focus on Article 16, we see that the Ministry of Interior, by law, deals with matters which concern -- and the very first matter is the implementation of the system for state and public security. If we stay on this exhibit for a moment and turn to Article 47(1), focus in on that, please, we see that Mr. Boskoski was responsible for the conduct of his employees as the Minister of the Ministry of Interior, pursuant to this same law, Article 47, which says, 47(1): "The work of a Ministry is managed by a Minister." And if we move now to Article 49, if we could focus on Article 49(1), we see that this law tells us: "The minister represents the Ministry, organises and secures the lawful and efficient completion of work and tasks, submits regulations and other acts for which he is authorised and undertakes other measures from the competence of the Ministry in accordance with the law; decides on the rights, duties and responsibilities of government employees and other individuals employed by the Ministry who do not have government employee status, unless otherwise stated by law." And finally, Your Honours, if we turn to 65 ter 88, which is the law on internal affairs for Macedonia that was in force in 2001, and we focus on Article 6, we see that the law says, the second part of that article: "An employee of the Ministry must implement orders of the Minister or the person authorised by him given in connection with the functions of the Ministry, except when implementation of the orders present a criminal offence." Ljube Boskoski's official responsibility, which included public and state security, also then included violations of the laws or customs of war. I'd like to show you briefly a portion of 65 ter number 83, which is an English translation of the Macedonian Criminal Code as it stood in 2001, and this is the table of contents. If we go to the next page -- no -- we see that Chapter 34 is entitled "Crimes Against Humanity and International Law." If we can turn to those chapters, please, the includes Article 403 to 417. Article 403 describes the crime of genocide. The title of Article 404 at the bottom of that page, "War crimes against the civil Population." If we can turn the page, please, we see Article 405, "War crimes against wounded and ill." And if we go to the next page. Article 406, "War crimes against prisoners of war." Article 407, "Use of unallowed combat needs." If we can move forward a page or two, to Article 417, please, and if we could focus on Article 417. This particular article codifies the crime of racial or other discrimination, Article 417, and notes in subparagraph 1: "A person who based on the difference in race, colour of skin, nationality or ethnic belonging, violates the basic human rights and freedoms acknowledged by the International Community, shall be punished with imprisonment of six months to five years." Ljube Boskoski exercised his de jure and de facto authority at many different levels of the Ministry of the Interior. For example, documents that will be presented to you during the course of the trial, demonstrate that Mr. Boskoski executed -- exerted his effective control down to minute details of police administration. If we can see Exhibit 36, please. This is a decision dated the 25th of May, 2001. If we can highlight the first paragraph, paragraph 1, please, the whole paragraph. We see that a Mr. Ungelof is being assigned to the duty of deputy commander of the special tasks unit, Tiger, at the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Macedonia. If we could go back to the next page, please. No, go to the next page. We see there at the end of this decision, it's stamped and signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we don't seem to have that on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have it now? We see this decision is signed by Ljube Boskoski as Minister of the Interior. If we can turn to 65 ter number 37, please. It's a decision dated 20 June 2001. We can focus on paragraph 1, please, the whole paragraph. We see a Mr. Ilic is being transferred from duty in the police station at Centar to duty as deputy commander in the police station of Mirkovci within the Department of the Ministry of Interior for the municipality of Cair. If we can go back to page 1, please. Next page, next page. We see this decision is -- no, this is the wrong decision. Next decision. Okay. Next page. We see it is signed -- if we go back one. The decision was signed by Ljube Boskoski. If we can go to the next exhibit, please. Here we have a document dated 26 June 2001, and if we could focus on the title and the first few paragraphs, please. This is called a decision on establishing police special unit of the Ministry of Interior. Paragraph 1: "The police special unit is being established for accomplishing special tasks." Paragraph 2: "The special unit is being established in order to protect security of the Republic of Macedonia in conditions of complicated security situation." And by the way, Your Honour, this is 65 ter number 48. Subparagraph 4: "The command of the special unit is composed of a commander of brigade, commander of battalion, commanders of companies, and commanders for logistical security." Can we go to the next page of this decision, please? Next page. And we see that this decision was signed by Ljube Boskoski as Minister of the Interior. Mr. Boskoski's exercise of effective control even reached the level of instructions for procedures on providing identity cards for reserve police officers. We can look at 65 ter number 87, please. And if we can highlight the title, please. This is dated July 2001, "Rules on the form and procedure for the issuing of a separate identification document to members of the reservist rank of the Ministry of the Interior. If we can go back to the first page, please. Next page. You see a series of rules about how these identification documents should be issued, when they should be issued. Next page, please. Several pages of rules. Next page, we'll go to the end. And we see, finally, underneath Article 7, that these rules were signed by Ljube Boskoski as Minister of the Interior. Mr. Boskoski would often review the police forces that were underneath his responsibility and authority. I'd like to show you two short clips without any sound that will show Mr. Boskoski reviewing special units of the Macedonian police forces during 2001. This is from 65 ter number 979.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see the arrival of the Minister, these men at attention, and Mr. Boskoski addressing his subordinates. The next clip is of a different ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see Mr. Boskoski addressing a large group with police personnel. That's fine, thank you. As a person with superior responsibility and with the knowledge of the occurrence of the crimes charged in the indictment, Ljube Boskoski had an obligation to investigate and establish the facts of the crimes, and to impose appropriate punitive and disciplinary measures on the perpetrators. Such an obligation was a continuing one, at least until such time as May 2002, when the prosecutor of this Tribunal informed the Macedonian authorities that she was exercising primacy over the crimes arising out of and following the Ljuboten attack in August of 2001. So what did Mr. Boskoski do? Your Honours, on the 13th of August, 2001, Ljube Boskoski created a so-called commission for the review of the circumstances and to analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of the Interior in order to repulse the armed attack of the terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten. The report provided by this commission is Prosecution 65 ter number 239, and if we can focus just on the first page, please, and the paragraph called "Subject" and "Originator." You'll see the long title of the report, and below that, that the commission was formed pursuant to a decision dated 13 August 2001. You'll hear testimony during the trial that this commission was made up of three high-ranking police officers who were subordinate to Ljube Boskoski. On the 4th of September, 2001, the commission issued this report, and I'd like to show you the opinion that they stated at the end -- that the commission members provided at the end of their report. Next page, next page, go back one. And if we can just focus on the first paragraph of that pane. We see just in the first sentence, Your Honour, the activities which were undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Interior -- I'll start again: "The activities, which were undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Interior to repulse the armed attacks of the terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten, are indispensable, justified and lawfully undertaken." This was the opinion of the so-called commission. The chairman of the commission, Goran Mitevski was the head of public security for the Ministry of the Interior and a direct subordinate and long-term associate of Mr. Boskoski. Your Honours, this so-called commission in fact did not carry out any investigation into the events at Ljuboten, as claimed in the report. Prosecution witnesses will describe how the three members of the commission never met, never interviewed witnesses or suspects, whether police, army or ethnic Albanian victims identified in connection with the Ljuboten operation. They never collected any oral or documentary evidence relating to the murders, cruel treatment and destruction of property that occurred on or after the attack. They followed no established rules of evidence and procedure and issued this single vague and perfunctory opinion. The Prosecution will demonstrate, therefore, that the accused Boskoski completely failed to exercise his duty to take necessary and reasonable measures to ensure that his subordinates who committed the crimes, alleged in the second amended indictment, were punished. The evidence presented at trial will show that only ethnic Albanian residents of Ljuboten were investigated and prosecuted for the events that occurred there in August 2001. However, there were a number of reasonable measures that Mr. Boskoski could have performed, and let me briefly describe several of them to you before I finish my remarks. Mr. Boskoski could have filed a criminal report. Pursuant to the rule book for conducting the affairs of the Ministry of the Interior, which is Prosecution Exhibit 370, as an authorised official under Article 103, Mr. Boskoski had a duty, upon reasonable suspicion that a crime had been committed, to undertake necessary measures in order to reveal the perpetrator of a crime and prevent escape, and to discover and secure any evidence and gather information. That same rule book at Article 167 provides a duty after that information is gathered, to submit a criminal report to the public prosecutor. Mr. Boskoski could have conducted an internal review within the Ministry of the Interior and terminated the employees responsible for the crimes. Under the Labour Relations Act, which is 65 ter 376, in conjunction with the law on internal affairs, a genuine commission could be established, assessed the responsibility of the employee, and prepare a proposal to the Minister for a decision. With respect to the use of fire-arms or means of physical force and coercion that were used by Mr. Boskoski's employees in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, reports should have been generated, and based on the authorities that I have mentioned to you, an investigation should have been conducted either through a criminal investigation or by an internal review. I'd like to briefly show you 65 ter 100, please, which is a decree on the use of means of coercion and fire-arms within the Ministry of Interior. And if we focus on Article 5, please. Article 5 says: "Before using any means of coercion or fire-arms, if the circumstances allow, the authorised person will identify him or herself and clearly warn the other person on the use of the means." If we can take a look at Article 27, please. Focus on Article 27. This is a chapter entitled "Reporting on the Use of Means of Coercion Or Firearms." Article 27 says: "An authorised person, who has used some means of coercion or a fire-arm, submits a written report to the immediately senior person in charge, who determines the basis, the justification and the correctness of the use of the means of coercion, i.e., the fire-arm." And the Prosecution will provide you with evidence, Your Honour, during the trial that these procedures were working even during the armed conflict days of 2001. There is no evidence, however, that these procedures were ever implemented with respect to the events in Ljuboten. Can we look -- go back to Article 9, please, of that same exhibit. Focus on Article 9: "An authorised person who violates the legal authorisation by using means of coercion or fire-arms will be prosecuted according to the legal regulations." If we take a look now at 65 ter 88, which is again the law on internal affairs, Article 38. If we can go to Article 38, please, and focus on that. I want to go to 65 ter number 88, the next exhibit. Okay. Article 38, please. Okay, up here. Again, we see that according to the law on internal affairs: "The reason, the justification and the regularity of the use of means of enforcement or fire-arms in each concrete case is evaluated directly by the responsible superior." Finally, Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski had a general duty to investigate as an authorised official and as a minister of the Interior, he had a duty to investigate the crimes that occurred in Ljuboten. Neither a genuine investigation or even a genuine request for one was initiated by Mr. Boskoski or members of the Ministry of the Interior in respect of the murders, cruel treatment and wanton destruction charged in the indictment. Despite such an obligation and Ljube Boskoski's knowledge of the crimes, the Prosecution's evidence will prove that neither Johan Tarculovski nor the police unit that he led in the unlawful attack on Ljuboten, nor any member of the police force that was involved in the murder, cruel treatment and wanton destruction of properties of the ethnic Albanian residents in Ljuboten was ever punished, disciplined or reprimanded in any way by Mr. Boskoski or any other member of the Ministry of Interior. Mr. Tarculovski continued in his employment with the Ministry of Interior throughout Mr. Boskoski's term of office. Your Honours, due to his failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators of the crimes committed in the village of Ljuboten, the Prosecution will ask you to find Mr. Boskoski criminally responsible as a superior, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. Your Honour, that concludes the Prosecution's opening remarks. I will sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Ms. Residovic, the Rules provide that a statement may be made at this point by the Defence of Mr. Boskoski. Is it intended to make one at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence, pursuant to Rule 84 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, will use its right to provide the opening statement before it starts presenting its own evidence.
